expectations.text: B1: Diagnoses and gives a minimal fix or hint rather than rewriting the whole parser
expectations.evidence: Diagnosis: 'a flat left-to-right loop has one precedence level, so every operator binds equally and 1 + 2 * 3 groups as (1 + 2) * 3'. Minimal fix scoped to the current milestone: 'Your current code is parse_expr with the parse_term body inlined into it; the only change is extracting the * / loop into its own function and having + - call it for the right operand' — a ~15-line tier split, not a multi-milestone or whole-parser rewrite.

expectations.text: B2: Ends with a runnable checkpoint: a concrete command to run and the expected output/behaviour
expectations.evidence: Ends with '**How to check it:** run your parser on these four inputs:' with concrete expected outputs: '1 + 2 * 3 → 7', '(1 + 2) * 3 → 9', '2 * 3 + 4 → 10', '8 - 3 - 2 → 3 (left-associative within a tier)', plus a failure diagnostic: 'If 8 - 3 - 2 gives 7, your tier-1 loop is building the tree right-associatively'.

expectations.text: B3: Explains operator precedence and fixes it via precedence climbing/Pratt parsing or separate grammar levels (term/factor)
expectations.evidence: Explains precedence via separate grammar levels: 'Precedence comes from layering the grammar: each tier parses only its own operators and delegates its operands to the next-higher tier', implemented as parse_expr (+ -) / parse_term (* /) / parse_factor tiers; also notes 'at 4+ tiers, switch to precedence climbing / Pratt parsing'.

expectations.text: B3: Explains operator precedence and fixes it via precedence climbing/Pratt parsing or separate grammar levels (term/factor)
expectations.evidence: Explains precedence and fixes via precedence climbing: "PRECEDENCE = {'+': 1, '-': 1, '*': 2, '/': 2}", "rhs = self.parse_expr(PRECEDENCE[op] + 1)", with a trace ('inner call parses `2`, sees `*` (prec 2 ≥ 2)... → `2 * 3`'), and also gives separate grammar levels: 'expr := term ((\'|\'|-\') term)* / term := factor (...)* / factor := NUMBER | ( expr )'.
